title: The Apparatus Strikes Back: Momentum Conservation and the Cost of Spatial Superpositions
authors: Lucas C. Céleri, Diogo O. Soares-Pinto, Daniel A. Turolla Vanzella
abstract: Preparing massive particles in coherent spatial superpositions is a central objective of modern quantum science, motivated by applications ranging from fundamental tests of quantum mechanics and gravity to quantum-enhanced sensing. The experimental difficulty of realizing such superpositions is usually attributed to environmental decoherence mechanisms whose impact depends on the details of the experimental implementation. Here we identify a universal constraint arising from momentum conservation and the quantum nature of the preparation apparatus. Any protocol that places a particle of mass $m$ in a spatial superposition with separation $d$ necessarily entangles the particle with the center-of-mass degree of freedom of the apparatus responsible for the splitting. The resulting recoil displacement, fixed by conservation of the mass dipole moment, reduces the coherence of the particle when the apparatus is not included as part of the quantum system. For an apparatus of mass $M$, preserving coherence requires the recoil displacement to remain smaller than the coherence length of the apparatus center-of-mass state, leading to a quantitative bound expressible as a constraint on its temperature and on how rigidly the apparatus is anchored to the laboratory frame. We analyze the implications of this bound for current matter-wave interferometry experiments, proposals for gravitationally mediated entanglement, and tests of quantum mechanics near the Planck scale. Our main result, which may seem counterintuitive, is that the recoil of even heavy macroscopic apparatuses can pose a surprisingly strong constraint on the coherence of spatial superpositions of particles with masses well below the Planck mass. Finally, we discuss why the resulting limitation should be regarded as a conservative estimate and under which conditions it can be interpreted as an instance of false decoherence.
summary: The authors derive a universal constraint showing that preparing large spatial superpositions of massive particles inevitably entangles the particle with the momentum recoil of the apparatus used for splitting. This entanglement causes decoherence in the measured particle state, setting a fundamental lower bound on experimental feasibility based only on conservation laws.
main_problem: The paper identifies a universal constraint on preparing massive particles in coherent spatial superpositions arising purely from momentum conservation when an apparatus is used for splitting.
main_result: Momentum conservation necessitates that the particle becomes entangled with the apparatus due to recoil, leading to a quantitative lower bound on achievable coherence even for macroscopic setups.
method: The analysis uses quantum state evolution operators and calculates the reduced density matrix of the particle by tracing out the apparatus degrees of freedom, quantifying coherence via relative entropy.
model_or_system: The system involves a massive particle ($m$) placed in superposition ($\pm d/2$) using an auxiliary apparatus of mass $M$. The analysis focuses on the entanglement generated between the particle and the apparatus's Center-of-Mass (CM) motion, modeled as harmonic oscillators.
key_observables: Coherence factor ($\chi_c$), relative entropy of coherence ($C_{rel}$), and the resulting bound relating $m$, $d$, $M$, and $T$.
important_parameters: Particle mass ($m$), separation distance ($d$), apparatus mass ($M$), temperature ($T$), and characteristic frequencies ($\omega$). The low-temperature limit yields a temperature-independent constraint.
main_assumptions: The analysis primarily assumes that only the CM degree of freedom of the apparatus participates in state preparation, ignoring internal vibrational modes (which would tighten the bound).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how coherence decreases with increasing particle mass and show contour plots mapping the momentum-conservation constraint on achievable superposition separation ($d/\lambda_C$) based on apparatus parameters.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the fundamental conservation law, derives the entanglement consequence for the reduced state, quantifies the resulting decoherence bound using CM motion, and finally discusses practical implications, including internal mode excitations and conditions for 'false' coherence loss.
why_interesting: This work provides a fundamental, model-independent constraint on quantum metrology experiments involving massive objects, linking macroscopic mechanics (momentum conservation) directly to microscopic quantum coherence limits. It is crucial reading for anyone designing next-generation matter-wave interferometers or gravity tests.

The transition from the high-coherence (yellow) to the low-coherence (dark-blue) region reflects the increasing distinguishability of the apparatus recoil states associated with the two branches of the spatial superposition of the particle. At any temperature, coherence decreases as the particle mass increases, illustrating the growing impact of particle-apparatus entanglement imposed by momentum conservation.
